Burning Rate Emulator (BRE):

PI: James G. Quintiere, Univ. of Maryland

1. Goal
Determine burning conditions on flat
surfaces in quiescent microgravity
2

In general
• The goal of this study is to establish the burning
conditions for materials in a quiescent environment.
• We seek to define the burning in terms of the heat of
gasification L by using a burning rate emulator (BRE),
which is a burner with controlled fuel supply.
3

– Pool fires in 1 g

in microgravity

able to support burning in
microgravity

Relationship to NASA Flammability
Tests 1 and 2
• The Upward Flame Propagation (Test 1) is the dominant
test for material flammability by NASA.
– It tests the flame propagation of a vertical sample 30 × 6.4 –
7.5 cm wide, under a small electric source heat flux of 75
kW/m2.
– The atmospheric conditions are controlled.
– Burn length and time are recorded.
– It is considered a pass-fail type test.
• The NASA Test 2: Cone Calorimeter with external heat
fluxes of 25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement information gained
from Test 1.
9

2. Background Microgravity
Studies
10

Background of Combustion in
Microgravity
• Experiments in Skylab (Ross, 2001; Kimzey, 1974) indicated sustained
burning of thin paper and plastics.
• More recent experiments indicate flame spread on thin paper and plastic
thin cylinders in microgravity (Ross, 2001).
• Opposed flow spread in a quiescent atmosphere has been shown to
depend on material, thickness, and oxygen concentration (Ross, 2001).
• The burning of candle flames on the MIR (Ross, 2001) last for periods
ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A spherical flame
formed around the wick.
• Droplet experiments by Kumagai and others (Ross, 2001).
• Small diameter jet flames of 0.4 – 2.7 mm yielded spherical flames of
durations from 150 – 300 s (Ross, 2001).
• Sunderland et al. (1999) recorded flames for port diameters up to 3.3 mm,
and Re from about 10 – 1700 in microgravity.
• Brahmi et al. (2005) used a gaseous burner to simulate burning in g. They
burned ethane over a 60  60 mm sintered bronze plate in O -N flowing
2 2
at velocities of 10 – 150 mm/s.
• Bustamante (2012) aircraft and drop data on flat liquid-fueled wicks.

Knowledge Lacking and Knowledge
to be Gained by Flight Tests
• The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the
range of steady burning conditions for condensed fuels
in microgravity. We will identify the associated material
properties and the real materials that are represented.
• Once established based on fuel properties, NASA Test 2
could be used as a basis for establishing comparable
properties for real materials. This could elevate the role
of NASA Test 2 over Test 1. This would close the loop of
using a ground-based test to assess the true
flammability of materials in microgravity.
37

Science Data End Products
Objective
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity
for CH /N and C H /N mixtures on porous circular
4 2 2 4 2
burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O /N
2 2
ambients with various pressures and ambient O
2
concentrations and pressures. Emphasize conditions that
can be related to diverse condensed fuels.
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of
O /CO (desired).
2 2
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction
limits.
38

Science Data End Products
Science Data End Products
1. • Color flame images and shapes.
• UV images.
• Surface temperatures and incident flame heat flux measurements.
• Radiation from the flame to the surroundings to estimate radiative
flux.
• Flammability mapping of quasi-steady burning as a function of heat
of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface temperature.
• Quasi-steady burning flux (burning rate per unit area) as a function
of significant properties, e.g., heat of gasification, heat of
combustion, and smoke point.
• Contour plots of soot temperature and filament temperature.
• Contour plots of soot volume fraction.
• Plots of radiant emissions versus time.
• Plots of chemiluminescent emissions versus time.
2. Same as for Objective 1.
3. Extinction limit map. 39

Justification for Extended-
Duration Microgravity
• The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft
owing to considerable g-jitter disturbances.
• Testing in NASA 5.2-s drop facility indicated possible approach to
steady burning.
• The longer duration testing in the ISS will facilitate the efficient
operation of the BRE to exploit a relatively quick record of results
over a range of flow rates. This will insure a complete
flammability map in microgravity.
40

Work conducted since last Aug
• Drop test

41

Response to panelist recommendation
• Recommend proposed ignition tests have a lower
priority. Ignition eliminated
• Prioritize the experimental diagnostics, to minimize
complications in running the experiment and
downloading data. Done
• Focus on small burner designs for multiple reasons. In
addition, a burner design with narrow external walls is
strongly encouraged. Test matrix emphasizes 25 mm
and we have reduced the edge effect.
42

Response to panelist recommendation
• Some repeated tests are recommended to establish
uncertainty bounds and increase scientific credibility.
Expect wide range of data points in flight.
• The temperature range for the burner is not defined in the
current science requirement documents. Take what we get.
In document, the burner surface, temperatures at 2
locations with a range of 30 – 500 °C.
• The priority on O and pressure conditions ought to be on
2
whatever the preferred conditions are for future space
flight. Drop experiments should also help prioritize the test
sequence. Included current NASA human flight atmosphere
in test matrix
43

Response to panelist recommendation
• Heat flux gauges need to be installed into the burner.
Engineering plans need to be developed to ensure that the
burner/heat flux gauge can be preheated to a minimum of
65 °C to avoid condensation. Expect the temperature to be
high enough without water cooling and we are recording it.
• Consider a wide angle radiometer for one of the lower
radiometers (inconsistent for present ACME plans) and
arrange the burner so that the radiometer cannot see the
burner surface. Yes we have
• It is strongly encouraged to reconsider the inclusion of this
diagnostic (O2 sensor). No but have GC to confirm
44

Response to panelist recommendation
• The proposed radiation measurements need to provide
a measure of the flame radiation alone. Yes trying to
do
• Improve justification for the selected fuel flow rates
(use simple calculations of flame surface areas, flame
curvature and flame burning rates and confirm in drop
experiments). ?? Confirmed by drop test
• Clarity is needed for the test matrix. Some of the ‘tests’
may actually be multiple tests. Revised the test matrix
45

Response to panelist recommendation
• Experiments should be performed at nearly the same oxygen
level. If tests at constant O are not possible, a method to
2
convert experimental results obtained at one
O concentration to another O level needs to be developed.
2 2
Hope to have a theory for that.
• As discussed above, a careful design of the burner, with a thin,
low conducting, outside wall should allow the flame to sit
closer to the burner and add stability to the flame tests.
Reduce the edge
• Fundamentally, there is no guarantee of achieving quasi-
steady flames. The PIs should consider how to collect and
interpret data sets for which flames are sustained, but
unsteady. Hope to have a theory to guide us
46

BRE Operational Sequence
Action Approx.
Time
1. Ensure that the appropriate burner is installed. Preflow the
burner fluent gas at the composition of the upcoming test point
to flush the plumbing system.
2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point
pressure and species compositions, as specified in the test
matrix. Conditions are obtained in four ways: from cabin air
(desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and
replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge.
3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of
5 minutes is required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed
conditions.
4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for
video cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring
measurements and wait 15 s.
